newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian T-bills open firmer amid currency gains.
newsitem.headline: Canadian T-bills open firmer amid currency gains.

text.p: Canadian T-bills opened mostly firmer in active trade on Monday amid gains in the Canadian dollar and a firmer tone in U.S. fixed-income markets, analysts said.

"It's a combination of two things. One is the improving trend in the currency here overnight. The improvement in U.S. fixed-income prices as well certainly helped psychology here as we began the day," said Doug Sannuto, managing director of Canada cash markets with Bank of Montreal.
Canada's three-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.24 percent from 3.27 percent at Friday's close.

The Canadian dollar rebounded slightly in overnight trading, opening at C$1.3969 (US$0.7159) versus Friday's close of C$1.3995 (US$0.7145). Dealers said they were starting to see light at the end of the tunnel for the battered currency, which weakened to two-year lows in recent sessions. The dollar's recent weakness had prompted speculation the Bank of Canada would be forced to hike short term interest rates in order to defend the currency.
In other prices, the six-month when-issued T-bill firmed to yield 3.54 percent from 3.60 percent at the close of trading on Friday.
The one-year T-bill firmed to yield 4.22 percent from 4.28 percent.
The call loan rate traded at 3.0 percent, the center of the Bank of Canada's 2.75-3.25 percent target range.
